guard all along, which is why 148 x86 rounds never reproduced it. Full account: roadmap, "stale
FreeLDR identity PTEs in recycled user page tables".

**The closure evidence, which is the part worth copying.** The original fix proved the *oracle*
went quiet (`MmDeleteRmap mapping-not-in-list` once per run → 0) and that
`ZwMapViewOfSection` gained two passes. It did NOT show the sweep-kill rate had gone, so that
was measured separately: **639 arm64 `-smp 1` kmtest rounds (2026-09-14 → 10-03) carry 0
`BUGCHECK 0x50` and 0 `0x1A` — both of this bug's stop codes — and 0 short sweeps out of the
582 with a known total**, against 42/85 finishing before. Plus one fresh probe-bearing sweep:
93/93 launched, ratchet holding, and **0 hits across all armed MM sites** (`MMGUARD`,
`FREEMAPPED`, `PFNMISMATCH`, `KSTACK`) in 15,144 serial lines.

**Silence is only a result once you prove the probe shipped** — a July soak's every
"under the probes" claim was vacuous because the probes landed four hours after the media was
frozen. Check the MEDIA, not the build dir: `strings qemu/ramdisk.img | grep -c
mapping-not-in-list` returned 4 for the run above. **And check the ARCH: a probe can be absent
by compilation, not by staging.** `mm_guard_trip!` is `#[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")]` — its
printer is an arm64 header macro — so all 14 `[MMGUARD]` sites expand to nothing on i386/amd64.
`strings build-<arch>/ntoskrnl/ntoskrnl.exe | grep -c MMGUARD`: arm64 **43**, amd64 **0**,
i386 **0**. Every "x86 is quiet at these sites" reading is therefore vacuous, and the three
ways a probe's silence lies now have the same one-line test — grep the artifact you actually
booted, per arch. **Disproven, don't re-chase:** an `rtl_heap`
translation bug; the free-while-mapped tripwire (negative); `MmInsertRmap`'s two silent returns
(probed, never fire — still wrong as silent degrades, but not this). This entry exists because
§9.96 first registered the flake with a plausible-but-unproven label — **a label is not a
diagnosis** — and it is kept after the fix because the two faces are the thing a reader will
recognise if anything like it returns.

### A boot that goes silent at one line may have changed output CHANNEL, not died

**Symptom:** the serial log stops dead after a specific line and nothing follows,
so that line reads as the crash site. x86 freeldr "died at
`[freeldr] Switching stack...`" for months on any non-ATAPI boot device, and the
conclusion written down was that the stack switch itself failed.

**Cause:** the code before that line printed via UEFI `ConOut`, which the serial
log carries; everything after it printed via `TRACE`/`WARN`, which it does not.
The boot was running fine and invisible. A `ConOut` probe placed immediately after
the switch printed, which took one boot to establish and overturned the whole
reading — the real failure was ~20 lines later, in `RunLoader`.

**Fix:** before believing a last-line-is-the-crash-site story, check whether the
NEXT code uses a different print path. The discriminator is cheap: put one probe
on the channel the log demonstrably carries, immediately after the suspect line.
If it prints, the line is a channel boundary, not a fault — and the probe is worth
keeping, because the next reader will otherwise draw the same wrong conclusion.

### Writes through a file mapping never reach the file: the dirty bit read after the PTE was cleared
**Symptom:** a file written only through a mapped view (`CreateFileMapping` + `MapViewOfFile`,
or `NtCreateSection` on a file handle) has the right size and is all zeros on disk, and after
the section is gone even a cached read returns zeros. `WriteFile` to the same volume works.
Setup extracts `reactos.cab` exactly this way, so 984 of 1042 installed files were
zero-filled. **Cause:** i386/amd64 `MmDeleteVirtualMappingEx` (`i386/page.rs`, which amd64
shares) did `OldPte = InterlockedExchangePte(PointerPte, 0)` and then read the dirty bit from
`(*PointerPte).Long`, which it had just zeroed. The C reads `OldPte.u.Hard.Dirty`. Every unmap
reported the page clean, the segment entry never became dirty, and `FreeSegmentPage` /
`MmCheckDirtySegment` had nothing to write. arm64 read `OldPte` and was correct. **Fix:** read
the returned old value. `tools/scan_read_after_clear.py` gates the shape at zero, and
`--payload fatprobe` (step mapped-write) checks the behaviour in about a minute. It found this
when the install smoke needed 12 minutes per try.

### Shutdown never reboots: `MiShutdownSystem` loops on pages that are not dirty
**Symptom:** the shutdown stops after `[PO] shutdown: MmShutdownSystem(0)`, with no write
failures. `[MM] MiShutdownSystem: pass N wrote 49417 dirty data-file page(s)`: the same count
every pass, and the pages it names live on the CD (`$PATH_TABLE$`, `REACTOS.CAB`), so they
cannot really be dirty. **Cause:** `ntkrnl_sys::mm::IS_DIRTY_SSE` tested `0x8`, the low bit of
the share count (mm.h: bits 3..11), not `0x2`. Every page mapped an odd number of times
looked dirty, the write "succeeded", and the "while dirty" loop never ended. It sat harmless
until the PTE-dirty fix above made the shutdown flush do real work. `ARM3/section.rs` carried
a whole private SSE encoding as well (swap bit inverted, share count at bit 2), unused.
**Fix:** use mm.h's encoding. `tools/scan_sse_helpers.py` evaluates every Rust `*_SSE` helper
against the macro on sample entries. Read the printed `sse` value against the bit layout
before trusting a predicate's verdict about it.

### RAM above 4 GiB: a loader cap was hiding four bugs, none in the loader
**Symptom.** amd64 with more than 4 GiB described (freeldr `MM_MAX_PAGE`): BAD_POOL_HEADER
(0x19, P1=5) from `IopCreateArcNamesCd`'s 2 KB CD buffer, then INACCESSIBLE_BOOT_DEVICE with
the CD reading as zeros, a hang in the q35 AHCI bus scan, and on BIOS boots MEMORY_MANAGEMENT
from `[MMGUARD] rmap.MmInsertRmap PFN MISMATCH` at the first user mapping in System. The
"physical memory" line (`[MM] physical memory: N MiB`) also over-counted: 4095 MiB on a box
with 2 GiB below 4 GiB, 17407 MiB on a 4 GiB BIOS guest.
**Cause.** Each was its own bug; the 4 GiB cap only kept every buffer and table low.
1. `MiIsMemoryTypeInvisible` (ntkrnl-sys `inline/mm.rs`) was ported as `>= LoaderMaximum`, so
   firmware-reserved ranges (PCI hole, VGA hole, a 1 TB reserved run on BIOS) counted as RAM.
2. uniata's 32-bit bounce (`DB_IO`) copied back to `AtaReq->DataBuffer` after completion had
   advanced it (overrun of the next pool block), and copied even when the transfer had fallen
   back to PIO (zeros over good data). Upstream marks the path `ASSERT(FALSE)`.
3. uniata stored a 64-bit HBA's first DATA page address as the AHCI command-table address
   (`ahci_base64`), and dropped the table's own high half. Upstream has both.
4. The HAL's AP-trampoline identity map (PML4[0], scratch pages typed `LoaderHALCachedMemory`)
   was never removed, so System's first low user mapping was built inside HAL tables that the
   PFN database (correctly, after 1) no longer tracks.
**Fix.** In place in each; see the commit for the list. The general lesson: when raising a
cap that "keeps things working", expect the bugs it was masking to be in everything that
touches addresses, and boot several sizes (QEMU BIOS at 4/12/32 GiB, `VIBEOS_QEMU_HOSTILE=mem`
and `q35,mem` for UEFI) before blaming the cap. A HAL bounce through map registers for 32-bit
scsiport masters looked right and broke uniata, which does its own bouncing: scsiport's
`IoFlushAdapterBuffers` then copies an untouched map buffer over the data.

### Other Mm one-offs
- **A registry/hive addition that "shouldn't matter" trips an early 0x50** `[§9.10]` — the
  config manager loads the hive early and growing it shifts everything. **Don't ship the hive
  change**; treat the deterministic same-line repro as a gift, and confirm causation by reverting
  only the hive line.
- **Timer-table base skew makes every relative wait over-wait 4–60×** `[§9.9]`. The NT timer
  table requires `InterruptTime / KeMaximumIncrement == KeTickCount`, both 0-based since boot.
  Zero KUSER `InterruptTime`, KUSER `TickCount` and the `KeTickCount` global on the first tick.
  Oracle: a one-shot probe in `KxSetTimerForThreadWait`.
- **arm64-only AV on every demand-zero fault** → SMSS 0x6A. **UEFI memory-map retry never
  converges on arm64** (UINTN hardcoded `u32`).
- **`NtCreateSection` 0x50 is a dropped `ProbeForRead`, not a deep-MM bug** `[§9.104]` — and the
  dropped probe **masked** the deeper arm64 exception-dispatch recursion beneath it. **A missing
  guard can hide the bug it would have exposed.**

---

## SMP: what a second CPU unmasks

`-smp 2` does not usually find SMP bugs — it finds **UP assumptions** that were always wrong.

### The governing rule: an IRQL raise is not a lock
> **"On QEMU's single vCPU, DISPATCH_LEVEL is full mutual exclusion" is false the moment a
> second CPU exists.** In any component a `-smp N` boot exercises, an IRQL raise is *not* a
> lock. `[§9.55]`

netstack's TDI transport relied on it for its queue → the `-smp 2` "TDI dgram upcall TIMED OUT"
NET_FLAKE. Fix: a real `KSPIN_LOCK` via `SpinLockGuard`. Second instance in the same commit.

Third instance, and the purest form of it: **arm64's `KeSynchronizeExecution` raised IRQL and
called the routine, and never touched `Interrupt->ActualLock`** — while i386
(`ke/i386/irqobj.rs`) and amd64 (`ke/amd64/interrupt.c`) both acquire it. That is the one
function in the DDK whose entire contract *is* mutual exclusion against a driver's ISR, so on
the SMP kernel it delivered exactly nothing; on UP the IRQL raise happened to be enough, which
is why it survived. When a per-arch port of a synchronisation primitive is shorter than its
siblings, the missing lines are the primitive.

Fourth, the other half of the third: once `KeSynchronizeExecution` took `ActualLock`, arm64's
**ISR dispatch (`KiDispatchInterruptArm64`) still called the ISR without it**, on a comment
calling the lock "vacuous" on a UP port. At `-smp 2` vioblk's completion interrupt ran on CPU 1
while `HwStartIo` was mid-submit on CPU 0, matched a token not yet recorded, and handed
virtio-drivers a zero-length buffer (`assert_ne!` in `queue.rs` `recycle_descriptors`). A lock
held on one side only is no lock: check the thread side AND the interrupt side.

### A dropped interrupt RESTORE: one CPU spins IF=0 on a lock while the holder waits for its TB ack
**Symptom:** amd64 `-smp 2` `HANG_TIMEOUT`, serial silent after `[user32] DllMain PROCESS_ATTACH`
(the WoW64 guest starting alongside). `hang-cpustate.txt`: CPU0 in `ki_tb_shootdown` waiting on
`KiTbFlushWaitCount`; CPU1 in `KxAcquireSpinLock` on `MmPfnLock` (via `MiMapViewOfDataSection`)
with `RFL=00000002` -- **IF clear**, so the shootdown IPI can never land. Two gates in 30 minutes
on 2026-10-05, then ten clean farm boots: timing-dependent, but not rare under gate load.
**Cause:** `KiSwitchKernelStack` (amd64 `stubs.rs`) translated the C's
`Eflags = __readeflags(); _disable(); ... __writeeflags(Eflags);` as a bare `cli`. It runs when a
thread first calls win32k (`KiConvertToGuiThread` swaps in a large stack), so every GUI
conversion ran `MmDeleteKernelStack` and all of `PsConvertToGuiThread` -- desktop-heap mapping,
PFN lock -- with interrupts off. Harmless on UP, which has no IPI to miss; latent since the
2026-02 KE translation. NT spins for the PFN lock with interrupts ON precisely so a TB flush from
the holder gets through. **Fix:** `KeDisableInterrupts()` / `KeRestoreInterrupts()` around the
stack swap, with a compiler fence (the restore's `sti` is a `nomem` asm). **Proved
deterministically, not by soak:** a `gdb probe` with a hardware breakpoint at
`PsConvertToGuiThread` read IF=0 on 6/6 entries before and IF=1 on 6/6 after. When a C body
brackets a region with a save/restore of flags or IRQL, diff the Rust for BOTH halves -- a sweep
of every Rust fn that disables interrupts without restoring found this one only.

### A thread "switching" to itself spins forever on its own SwapBusy
**Symptom:** amd64 `-smp 2` `HANG_TIMEOUT` after a 60 s `[WIN32K] STUCK SEND`, one CPU idle in
`hlt`, the other parked at `.SwapBusySet` (`ctxswitch.S:181`) with **`RDX == R8`** in
`hang-cpustate.txt` — `KiSwapContextInternal`'s old and new thread are the same KTHREAD. Usually
preceded by `[RQRUNNING] queuing a RUNNING thread ... runningOnCPU=<this CPU>`. 1 of 3 boots with
each vCPU pinned to its own host core (`stress --profile starved-smp --cores 2`), 2026-10-09.
**Cause:** NT's wait-commit releases the dispatcher lock before `KiSwapThread` dethrones the
waiter, so a cross-CPU readier may legally queue the still-running thread T onto T's own CPU;
`KiSwapThread` then selects T. T set its own `SwapBusy` on the way in (every wait path calls
`KiSetThreadSwapBusy`), the asm spins until the NEW thread's `SwapBusy` clears, and only
`KiSwapContextResume` — after the spin — would clear it. Upstream's `CONFIG_SMP` never ran this.
The §9.56 work found the mechanism in July and armed a 0x57 tripwire, which is off by default, so
every unarmed boot still wedged silently. **Fix:** `KiSwapThreadImpl` treats NextThread ==
CurrentThread as "keep running": release `SwapBusy` and report a deliverable kernel APC exactly as
`KiSwapContextResume` would, skip the stack/CR3/TEB switch that is already T's. Proved by the path
firing, not by a soak going quiet: `[SMP] self-swap #1 resolved in place on CPU1` followed by
`CreateProcessW returned` and the desktop (run 20261009-210915-89vskrzs).

### A lock the C declares and never takes is a race the C never hit
**Symptom:** arm64 `-smp 2`, 1 boot in 5: BUGCHECK 0x1E in `CmpCreateKeyControlBlock` reading
a garbage `CM_KEY_NODE`, while the other CPU loops in `HvFreeCell` on a NULL bin.
**Cause:** registry writers on different keys hold the registry lock only shared, so two CPUs
ran `HvAllocateCell` on one hive; `HvpAddBin` swapped and freed the flat `BlockList` under every
reader. `CMHIVE.HiveLock`/`HiveLockOwner`, the lock Windows uses for exactly this, are declared
and initialized in ReactOS and never acquired. Upstream is mostly run on one CPU, where this is
invisible.
**Fix:** take the declared lock (cmlib-rust `hivelock.rs`). Prove it with a stressor that
drives the two sides together and an A/B with the lock compiled out: `regstress` turned a
1-in-5 boot flake into 2/2 crashes in seconds without the lock, 0 failures with it. A grep for a
struct's lock fields with no acquirer is a cheap sweep for more of these.

**Corollary — a stressor finds the next lock bug too.** The same run hung on a push-lock release
(`ExfReleasePushLock[Shared]` adopted a failed CMPXCHG's value in only one of its two arms; a
port of an upstream fix that missed half of it) — a livelock no smoke boot had shown except as
an unexplained HANG_TIMEOUT. A new hot lock exercises the lock primitive's slow paths far more
than boot ever did.

### An object linked into a shared list before it is initialized
**Symptom:** amd64 `-smp 2`, about 1 boot in 5 at worst: BUGCHECK 0x1E reading NULL+0x90 in
win32k `ProcessTimers`, on the raw input thread, after the desktop is up.
**Cause:** `CreateTimer` linked a zeroed TIMER into `TimersListHead` and `IntSetTimer` filled it
in afterwards, both without `TimerLock`, while the RIT walks that list under `TimerLock` every
10 ms. On one CPU the walker can never run inside that window. On two it can: if the creating
vCPU stalls for two ticks, one pass drives the zeroed countdown negative and the next reads
`pti->TIF_flags` with `pti == NULL`. Upstream ReactOS has the identical code.
**Fix:** link only after every field is set, under the lock the walker holds. The tell on a live
VM: walk the list and look for an entry whose fields are all still zero except the ones the
walker writes. When a C "create" helper links the object it returns, check whether anything
walks that list on another thread.

### A busy check that drops the request instead of handing it to the CPU that is busy
**Symptom:** amd64 `-smp 2`, ~7% of gate boots and ~0% solo: the boot goes silent at a
different place each time (services START, `CreateProcessW`, csrss `LoadServerDll`), both CPUs
idle in `KiIdleLoop`, no fault. Every stuck thread is waiting for an I/O on the boot volume
(cdfs on the USB stick): a page-in at APC_LEVEL, or a create whose check-verify IOCTL is
pending in disk.sys/classpnp. The xHCI controller is idle with nothing on its event ring.
**Cause:** two copies of one bug, both in upstream ReactOS C, faithfully translated. A path
finds the work "already being done" and returns, while the CPU doing it has already passed the
point where it would have noticed the new work.
- usbport `USBPORT_FlushPendingTransfers`: `FlushPendingLock` was a try-lock (CAS 0 -> 1, else
  return). A transfer queued while another CPU was finishing a flush of the same endpoint was
  never flushed. Live state: one transfer on the bulk endpoint's `PendingTransferList`,
  `TransferList` empty, lock 0, endpoint idle, `WorkerList` empty (2 of 3 kept VMs).
- usbstor `USBSTOR_QueueNextRequest`: returned early when `ActiveSrb` was set. A request arriving
  between the finishing request's `QueueTerminateRequest` and that check claims `ActiveSrb` and
  `IoStartPacket`s behind the StartIo slot the finished request still holds, and nobody calls
  `IoStartNextPacket`. Live state: FDO `CurrentIrp` a freed (recycled) IRP, device queue `Busy`
  with one IRP whose SRB is `ActiveSrb`, `IrpPendingCount` = 1 + the `IrpList` (1 of 3).

On one CPU neither window opens: the finishing side runs at DISPATCH_LEVEL start to end.
**Fix:** hand the work over instead of dropping it. The flush lock is now a request count: a
caller that finds it held increments it and leaves, and the holder makes another pass unless
the count is still exactly its own. `QueueNextRequest` releases the slot
(`IoStartNextPacket`) when its caller retired the slot owner, so the claimant starts. The
cancel routines retired requests that never held the slot and keep the C behaviour, because
releasing it there would start a second command beside the running one. Sweep for the shape:
`if (InterlockedCompareExchange(&X, 1, 0)) return;` or "if busy, return" with no re-check
after the holder releases. Also the counter form, `if (InterlockedIncrement(&X) != 0) {
InterlockedDecrement(&X); return; }` with `X` starting at -1, which a CAS grep misses. A skip is
only a bug when nothing retries it: usbport's `EndpointWorker` returns TRUE when busy and its
callers put the endpoint back on `WorkerList`, and `DpcHandler`'s skip of a busy endpoint is
re-polled by the 500 ms `USBPORT_TimerDpc`. The repo-wide sweep (2026-10-11: CAS and counter
try-locks, busy-flag early returns, every `IoStartPacket` driver, usbxhci's ISR-to-DPC latches)
found no third instance.
**Finding it** took the IRPs, not the census. The census's `Suspended=1` was usbport's worker
thread, which waits with `Suspended` as a generic wait reason (so do kbdclass, mouclass, atapi
and iomgr), and it was in 42 of 44 hang histograms only because passing boots end before the
census prints a histogram. Do this instead on a kept VM: stuck thread -> `ETHREAD.IrpList` ->
the IRP's current stack location names the device holding it -> that driver's queue state.
`[KRNLBASE]` gives the kernel base; an attach-on-fail manifest now records it, because without
it every `gdb inspect` runs find-kbase's page scan and times out over the windows-host stub.
For a driver-private struct offset, compile `const _: [(); 0] = [(); 1_000_000 +
offset_of!(T, f)];` against the crate's `types_<arch>.rs`: the error message prints it.

### A UP-tuned boot timeout reads an `-smp N` boot as a wedge
**Symptom:** an `-smp N` run fails the boot fixture with a plain `TimeoutError` while the serial
log shows the boot still *talking* — arm64 `-smp 2` conformance reached
`[WINLOGON] explorer.exe created (PID 216)` and was mid-SCM-startup when the 180s budget expired.
**Cause:** the per-arch `boot_timeout` is sized against the *UP* boot (arm64: ~40s observed →
180s budget). Under MTTCG every vCPU is its own host thread doing its own translation, and the
guest genuinely does more work (AP bring-up, IPI round-trips, real spinlock contention), so
wall-clock to any milestone grows roughly linearly in N — on an already-contended fleet host,
more. **Fix:** `vm.smp_boot_timeout()` scales `boot_timeout` by N. Scale the CLOCK only —
`hang_silence_seconds` is deliberately NOT scaled, because the silence watchdog is what actually
catches a wedge, so a genuine MP hang still fails in ~120s instead of burning the stretched
budget. Do not "fix" this by lowering the boot marker; the marker is what proves the desktop
came up. Recompute the scale from a stashed UP value, not from the current one, or a config
reused across a retry loop multiplies each time.

### On a GICv3, every IPI of the early-SMP window is lost until the distributor is enabled
**Symptom:** arm64 `--gic 3 --smp 4` hangs right after `KeStartAllProcessors: 4 processor(s)
online` with `[IPI] KeIpiGenericCall stuck in arrival: ... TargetSet=e`. Every AP printed
`[GIC] CPUn percpu (GICv3): ... awake=1 SRE=1 SGI0 enabled=1`, so each redistributor was found,
woken and had the IPI enabled. **Cause:** a GICv3 distributor's group enables (GICD_CTLR
EnableGrp1/ARE) gate SGIs and PPIs as well as SPIs, even though SGIs and PPIs live in the
redistributors. UEFI leaves the distributor disabled at ExitBootServices, and the BSP turns
it on only at clock init (Phase 1), well after the AP self-test IPI. The GICv2 path never hit
this because each AP's per-CPU init already wrote GICD_CTLR. **Fix:** per-CPU init enables
the distributor (idempotent, through the loader's identity map of its first page), and the
BSP's affinity is recorded at HalInitSystem, so an early IPI to it pends instead of having
no route (`hal-rust arm64/gic3.rs`).

### Dropped `#ifdef CONFIG_SMP` blocks are TIME BOMBS, not dead code `[§9.95]`
`KiRetireDpcList`'s SMP-only deferred-ready drain was dropped in translation, so **an idle CPU
re-HLTs with runnable threads parked on its own `DeferredReadyListHead`** → `KeGuardedMutex`
kmtest TIMEOUT. **The census cracked it before GDB did** — `ke/census.rs` (a 10s sync watchdog)
printed "CPU 1 asleep in `hlt` with a runnable thread on its own deferred list." **Sweep every
`CONFIG_SMP` block in the C for one that never made it across.**

### The SwapBusy context-swap protocol was inverted/unenforced `[§9.94]`
NT's MP-only swap-busy protocol has three parts and i386 had none of them; amd64 had one. The
invariant: **a dying thread's stack cannot be freed until the thread is off every CPU**, and the
release must happen **after ESP has left the old stack.** Four edits: acquire-spin in
`KiSwapContextEntry`, release-clear in `KiSwapContextExit`, `KiSetThreadSwapBusy` before the
swap in `KiDispatchInterrupt` (both x86 arches), and a spin in `PspReapRoutine`/
`PspDeleteThread` (all arches). This closed the kernel-stack `IN_PAGE_ERROR` teardown race that
a system-PTE leak had been masking `[§9.88]` — **the leak fix unmasked the race, so it looked
like a new bug.**

### i386 SMP bring-up: three offset/layout bugs, each masked in UP `[§9.91]`
Swapped `PRCB_BUILD_*` constants → 0x79 MISMATCHED_HAL; `KDESCRIPTOR` missing its `Pad` field →
0x1E in `memcpy`; the loader block written by raw pointer → 0x50 with a masking 0x1E cascade;
and a cdecl worker handed to an NTAPI slot.

### The IPI-packet protocol trio `[§9.101]`
**An EMPTY "wait for completion" block** (`KeFlushEntireTb`'s SMP tail read as a comment and
translated as nothing — the *empty-wait-comment* class), **`IPI_FREEZE` treated as a request bit
when it is a STATE** (so the freeze request corrupted its own state machine), and a
scheduler-oracle mark with one uncovered promote site. **An oracle is only as good as its unmark
coverage.**

### First `-smp 2` boot: two latent bugs `[§9.51]`
uniata's `CPU_num > 1` switch to an nIEN-gated ATAPI path breaks under QEMU (gate it on bare
metal), and five+ hand-rolled `KUSER_SHARED_DATA` shadows with fantasy offsets → 0x4C. **Trap
for the debugger: uniata AND scsiport are both Rust translations**, so "the driver is C, it must
be the kernel" is wrong.

### Un-parking the AP into the scheduler `[§9.52]`
Four rules: per-processor Phase-1 loops must run **after** `KeStartAllProcessors`; the trap.S
interrupt stub's **handler** owns the IRQL protocol; **TLB-shootdown senders must poll-service,
never just wait**; and skipping the round-trip for `hlt`ed CPUs (lazy-idle TLB) is a large win
— **but only if EVERY way out of `hlt` services the deferral before running anything**, including
device ISRs (next entry: one path did not, and it corrupted amd64 memory silently).

### Successful reads that leave their pages ZERO: a lazy-TLB CPU ran a device ISR
**Symptom** (amd64 `-smp 2`, roughly half of boots; i386 never): faces with nothing in common —
csrss `0xC000001D` twice at the *same* address (int3 padding after an import thunk, the caller's
return address still at `[rsp]`), `0x6B` with `STATUS_DISK_CORRUPT_ERROR`, a kernel `0x1E`
executing at `0x8f654`, `0x4C`/`STATUS_INVALID_IMAGE_FORMAT`, double faults inside
`RtlVirtualUnwind` (the dispatcher unwinding from a garbage PC until the stack ran out), and
silent hangs. Boots that reached the desktop carried the corruption too.

**Cause:** amd64's lazy-idle TLB protocol lets a shootdown sender skip any CPU blocked in `hlt`
on the premise that it "touches only stable kernel mappings". A device interrupt wakes that CPU
and `KiInterruptDispatch` runs the ISR at once — and the IDE ISR copies PIO sector data through
the system-VA mapping of the request's MDL, a VA the system-PTE pool had recycled while this CPU
still held the old translation. The data went to the OLD physical page: the read's own pages
stayed zero (they come zeroed from `MmRequestPageMemoryConsumer`) while whatever now owned the
old page was overwritten. Only idle-exit and the DPC ISR serviced the deferral.

**Fix:** `KiInterruptDispatch` calls `KiTbLazyIdleExitForInterrupt` before the ISR
(`ke/amd64/ipi.rs`). Measured: 8/8 `-smp 2` boots to desktop with zero corrupt reads, against
9/16 and 15 zero pages in 3 of 4 boots before.

**How it was found, which is the reusable part:** the faces were too varied to chase one at a
time, so the probes went where the bytes are decided rather than where they are used. `[KI-EXC]`
printing the code bytes at RIP turned "illegal instruction" into "this page is zeros"; a scan
after `IoPageRead` in `MmMakeSegmentResident` then showed full 16 KB reads succeeding with zero
pages, every one on CPU 1, against a `-smp 1` control whose only zero reads were single genuine
tail sectors. **Diff the SMP probe output against a UP control before reading it** — half the
first listing was legitimate zeros.

### User pages lost after a decommit: MM flushed only its own CPU's TLB
**Symptom** (arm64 `-smp 2`, regstress, about 1 boot in 3): the process stops mid-run with
both CPUs idle. The real event is earlier: a user access violation inside ntdll's heap, on
metadata that reads back as zero (`RtlpRemoveFreeBlock` on a free entry with `Size` 0, so the
hint index is `0xFFFFFFFF`; `RtlpInsertFreeBlockHelper` following a NULL `Flink`). The page
under the bad entry is entirely zero while the next page is properly decommitted.

**Cause:** `MiProcessValidPteList` (decommit), `MiDeletePte`, `MiRemoveMappedPtes` and
`MiFlushTbAndCapture` free or change user mappings and then call `KeFlushCurrentTb`, exactly
as the ReactOS C does. That only flushes the calling CPU. A thread of the same process on the
other CPU keeps the old translation, writes into a frame MM has already freed, and the heap's
own CPU recommits the VA to a fresh zero page. The data is lost on one side and lands on the
frame's next owner on the other (kernel pool included).

**Fix:** `KeFlushProcessTb` at those sites (broadcast `tlbi vmalle1is` on arm64, the
shootdown on x86 SMP), before the PFN lock is released. `KeFlushCurrentTb` is local by
contract; any caller that just changed a mapping another CPU may hold is a bug.

**How it was found:** the hang capture looked like a scheduler wedge, and a timer-table
watchdog chased that for hours. What broke it was splitting failing boots from passing ones
on a single fact (`[UEXC]` after `[REGSTRESS] start`: every failure, no pass), then probing
the corrupt page itself: a page that is ALL zero is lost memory, not an overwrite.

### A `FAULT LOOP` with a valid PTE: the AP never left its boot TTBR0
**Symptom** (arm64 `-smp 2`): `*** FAULT LOOP (FATAL): the pager reported success on the
same fault` on a user-half VA while the faulting thread is a System thread, then
`PspInitializeSystemDll FAILED subcode=7` and BugCheck 0x6B. In the `[FAULTLOOP]` dump the
PDE/PTE read through the self-map are valid, but `AT(VA)` reports a **level-0** fault and
**TTBR0 != TTBR1**.

**Cause:** an AP leaves the HAL trampoline with TTBR0 = its temporary identity map.
`KiSwapProcess` reloads TTBR0 only when the process changes, and every System thread shares
the idle process's directory, so nothing ever replaced it. The pager checks the System
process's tables, the hardware walks the identity map, and the fault can never be satisfied.
It stayed latent while threads rarely ran on the AP; fixing `KiIdleSummary` (threads now go to
the idle CPU) took it from never to 3 of 4 boots.

**Fix:** `KiSystemStartupBootStack` installs the idle process's directory in TTBR0 and TTBR1
on each AP, as `KiSwapProcess` would. **Tell:** `KiSwapProcess` sets both registers to the
same table, so TTBR0 != TTBR1 on a running CPU means TTBR0 was never set by a process switch.

### A kernel write to a read-only page succeeds, but only on an AP: CR0.WP never set there
**Symptom** (i386 `-smp 2`): kmtest `ZwMapViewOfSection` :492 writes to a PAGE_READONLY
view under SEH and gets no access violation, every sweep; it passes on one vCPU.
**Cause:** without CR0.WP, supervisor writes ignore the PTE's R/W bit. `KiSetCR0Bits` runs
from `KiInitMachineDependent` (`KeInitSystem`), once, on the current CPU, and Phase 1 calls
`KeStartAllProcessors` BEFORE `KeInitSystem`, so the APs copied a CR0 that did not have WP
yet. The C has the same order. **Fix:** set it inside `KiInitMachineDependent`'s
per-processor affinity loop. **Generalize:** any per-CPU control-register or MSR setup done
in a Phase 1 routine that runs on one CPU is an AP gap; check where the AP's copy came from.

### A DPC queued on a CPU never runs until it idles: `DpcInterruptRequested` stuck at 1
**Symptom** (arm64 and i386 `-smp 2` only): kmtest `KeDpc` reads `DpcCount = 0` after every insert
and the re-insert returns FALSE; the DPC sits queued until that CPU next reaches its idle loop.
**Cause:** every IPI_DPC sets `Prcb->DpcInterruptRequested`, including the ones
`KiDeferredReadyThread` sends only to wake a CPU for a thread. The arm64 soft-interrupt body
(and i386's `KiDispatchInterrupt`) cleared it only when it retired a non-empty queue, so a
wake with nothing queued left it set,
and `KeInsertQueueDpc` skips requesting an interrupt while it is set. **Fix:** clear it on the
empty-queue path too. Any per-PRCB "request pending" flag needs a clear on every path that
services the request, not just the path that finds work.

### A multi-CPU guest is several times slower and both CPUs are mostly halted: the wake IPI is masked
**Symptom** (amd64 `-smp 2` only): boot and every kmtest launch take ~3-4x the 1-vCPU time,
yet timers run at the right rate (sleep-bound tests take their nominal time). Tests that
assume a thread they started has reached its wait within 10 ms fail (`ExResource` waiter
counts). Sampling both vCPUs over gdb (`info threads` per attach, then reading each
PRCB through `$gs_base`/`$k_gs_base` + 0x180) finds a CPU **halted in its idle thread with
`NextThread` already set**.
**Cause:** amd64 `KiIpiSend(IPI_DPC)` sends the DISPATCH soft vector 0x2F. On amd64 IRQL
*is* the APIC TPR (CR8), and the idle loop blocks in `hlt` at DISPATCH_LEVEL, so vector 0x2F
(priority class 2) is held pending in the IRR and `hlt` never returns until a higher-class
interrupt -- the clock tick -- arrives. Every cross-CPU handoff costs up to a tick. i386 and
arm64 send IPI_DPC through their real IPI vector and never saw it.
**Fix:** also ring the 0xE1 IPI vector, which is above every IRQL the idle loop runs at; its
handler services nothing, but `hlt` returns and the idle loop re-checks `NextThread` and its
DPC queue. Keep the 0x2F request: it is what preempts a *busy* target once its IRQL drops.
Don't filter the wake to CPUs in `KiTbLazyIdleSet`: the idle loop joins that set after its
`NextThread` check, so a filtered wake races. A wake interrupt must be deliverable at the
IRQL the sleeper sleeps at.

### The machine keeps running after a BUGCHECK: the other CPUs were never frozen
**Symptom** (MP, both amd64 and arm64): the serial carries thread exits, network
self-tests and DLL loads *after* the `*** BUGCHECK` line, interleaved with the flight
recorder dump. The crash record describes a machine that was still changing.

**Cause:** arm64's `KxFreezeExecution` was an empty stub, so a bugcheck stopped nothing.
amd64's was real but ran where the C puts it, after `KeBugCheckWithTf`'s trap-frame scans
and flight-recorder dump, which take long enough under TCG for other CPUs to do real work.

**Fix:** arm64 implements the freeze (staged `IpiFrozen` states, SGI delivery, target side
in `KiIpiServiceRoutine`); with no NMI, the owner's wait is bounded and names any CPU that
did not stop. amd64 and arm64 freeze at the top of `KeBugCheckWithTf`, right after the
banner, so a hung freeze still leaves the crash code. Not i386: its freeze rides a maskable
vector with an unbounded wait. Because amd64's NMI freeze can park a CPU while it holds the
HIGH_LEVEL print lock, `KdbpAcquireLock` takes that lock by force after a bounded spin once
a bugcheck is active. **Verify with `--tripwire FREEZE_SELFTEST=1 --smp 4`:** a ticker on
the last CPU must stop within one line of the banner (measured: one tick, then only the
dump, on both arches).

### The ready-list tear: five refuted theories and the one real hole `[§9.56]`
**FIXED** (all three arches; 0 occurrences across every post-fix boot). The long hunt is the
lesson, so keep the shape: `Prcb->DispatcherReadyListHead[pri]` (8/9 observed) was found torn,
with faces `0x1E` IN_PAGE_ERROR, `0x19` BAD_POOL_HEADER, `0xF4`, and silent wedges — ~0.9%
organically, ~35% under the `cswitchdep` amplifier.

**Root cause: `KiIdleLoop` read, nulled and promoted `Prcb->NextThread` LOCK-FREE**, inherited
verbatim from ReactOS's never-validated `CONFIG_SMP` C (i386 *and* amd64 both lacked the
acquire). `KiDeferredReadyThreadImpl`'s standby-displacement branch — correctly under the PRCB
lock — read `NextThread = T` while the idle CPU concurrently promoted T to Running, then marked
the *running* T DeferredReady and re-deferred it; T later requeued itself run-side while still on
a drain chain, tearing the double links. **Every other promote site already held the lock; idle
was the single hole.** Fix: acquire the PRCB lock, **re-check `NextThread` under it** (a
displacement may have consumed it), promote, release, *then* `sti`.

> **A field guarded by lock L at N−1 of N sites is not guarded.** Grep every reader and writer of
> a scheduler field before concluding the locking is sound — and **treat every inherited
> `CONFIG_SMP` primitive as unreviewed**, because upstream never ran it.

**Five theories refuted with evidence first — do not re-derive them** (~40 min each):
1. **SwapBusy wait-side unimplemented** — the amd64 run-side spin *already exists in assembly*
   (`ctxswitch.S`), and a `.rs`-only grep missed it. **Grep the asm before declaring anything
   unimplemented.** (i386 genuinely has no spin — a separate latent gap, not this bug.)
2. **Double-queue on an already-Ready thread** — fired once, then later tears happened with the
   guard **silent**, which proves **`State` is the WRONG PREDICATE**: a path can change `State`
   without unlinking. This was the headline theory for weeks and it was wrong.
3. **Union-alias clobber** — `KTHREAD.__bindgen_anon_3` really *is* a union, so
   `KiInsertDeferredReadyList`'s `SwapListEntry.Next` write really *does* alias
   `WaitListEntry.Flink`. Beautiful theory; a precise still-linked guard was silent. **It never
   happens.**
4. **Already-linked node re-inserted** — a state-independent linkage test ("do my neighbours
   point back at me?") was silent.
5. **Missing/wrong PRCB lock at a mutator** — audited; every mutator pairs with the correct
   PRCB's lock, and the dispatcher lock is real too.

**Two false oracles in one hunt, both of which cost real time:**
- `cswitchdep` is a repro **AMPLIFIER, not a detector** — its violation output is noise under
  `-smp N` (a single global held-count with no per-CPU separation mis-fires on most switches).
  **It amplifies; it does not pin.**
- The attribution table's own hash lied: `rq_inflight_mark()` CAS-inserted at the first empty
  probe slot *before* finishing its 8-slot scan, so a legal re-mark created a duplicate twin that
  later fired a false violation. **In an open-addressed probe table, insert-at-first-empty may
  only happen after a full-window scan for the key** — and **a diagnostic that bugchecks must be
  held to the same correctness bar as the kernel it polices.**

**The method that finally worked:** stop adding tripwires and catch the corrupting *store*.
Enriched forensics that named it — report *which* CPU's list a thread is wrongly linked into plus
its state and owning PRCB, and dump the corrupted link *value* — turned "the list is torn" into a
specific traceable invariant ("a Running `CurrentThread` is simultaneously linked in a ready
list"), from which the upstream writer followed.

---

## arm64: SEH, unwind & bring-up

### arm64: uncached RAM mapped as Device memory alignment-faults on a merged store

**Symptom:** BUGCHECK 0x1E on arm64 only, in a driver writing to its own DMA buffer. ESR
`0x96000061` (data abort, DFSC 0x21 alignment fault), an odd FAR, and `[ALIGN]` showing PTE
AttrIndx 1. atapi's SATL faulted building a VPD page: `stur w9, [x8, #5]`.
**Cause:** `MiPlatformCacheAttributes`'s RAM row mapped `MmNonCached` to `MiNonCached`, which on
arm64 is MAIR slot 1, Device-nGnRnE. Device memory faults on any unaligned access, and LLVM merges
the C's byte stores into unaligned word stores freely. The buffer came from
`MmAllocateContiguousMemorySpecifyCache(…, MmNonCached)`; x86 never notices, because PCD
memory has no alignment rule.
**Fix:** on arm64 the RAM row maps uncached types to `MiWriteCombined`, which is MAIR slot 2,
Normal Non-cacheable. That is what Linux uses for coherent DMA, and it never aliases RAM with a
Device type. I/O space keeps Device.

### arm64 HAL: a DMA adapter must report map registers for the length asked

**Symptom:** every AHCI port fails START with `0xC000009A`, and pciidex prints
`CH n: Unable to allocate DMA memory`.
**Cause:** the arm64 HAL's `new_adapter` reported 256 map registers whatever the
`DEVICE_DESCRIPTION` said. Drivers size per-transfer tables from that number. pciidex's AHCI
command table (128 bytes plus 16 per entry) became bigger than a page, it packed zero tables per
page, and it asked for a 0-byte common buffer.
**Fix:** report `BYTES_TO_PAGES(MaximumLength) + 1` for a bus master and 1 otherwise, as
`x86/dma.rs` does. "Map registers are free here" is true of the hardware, not of the contract.

### A UEFI boot with no display hangs in the loader (and then bugchecks 0xB4)
- **Symptom:** with no display device (a server; `smoke --arch arm64 --headless`) the
  serial log stops at `[FLDR] past _changestack, entering RunLoader` with the CPU in
  firmware code, then, once that is fixed, at a `!!FREELDR-RUST-PANIC@...ui.rs`, then
  at `BugCheck 0xB4` (VIDEO_DRIVER_INIT_FAILURE) after `[arm64vid] No ARC framebuffer`.
  Seen 2026-10-08 preparing for EC2 Graviton, which has no display.
- **Cause:** four independent gaps, each hidden by every rig having a framebuffer:
  1. **A dropped `#ifdef UEFIBOOT`.** ui.c falls back to the no-UI vtable when the text
     UI cannot start; the translation kept only the BIOS `return FALSE`, with a comment
     claiming UEFIBOOT was off. It is the crate's `uefi` feature, on for uefildr.efi.
  2. **A zero-byte allocation.** With no display the framebuffer console's buffer size
     is 0; `MmAllocateMemory(0)` reports itself through the text UI being initialized,
     whose message box waits for a key on UEFI's console input forever. The C does the
     same.
  3. **A divide by zero C gets away with.** `UiIndicateProgress` divides by a progress
     count only `UiInitProgressBar` sets; arm64 `udiv` by zero quietly yields 0, Rust
     panics.
  4. **No display, no win32k.** arm64vid bailed with no firmware framebuffer, as if a
     VGA miniport would take over; arm64 has none.
- **Fix:** restore the UEFI fallback under `cfg(feature = "uefi")`; no display, no
  off-screen buffer; guard the division; arm64vid runs the desktop on a 1024x768 frame
  in nonpaged memory (`Arm64VidHeadless`). The loader now says
  `[FLDR] waiting for a key on the UEFI console` before blocking on one, since on a
  headless machine that wait is the hang.

### `RtlVirtualUnwind` decoding and the frame-walk bugs
- **`save_next` resolves FORWARD, not backward** `[§9.114]` — a **32%-wrong** decoder that
  silently mis-restored callee-saved registers. ARM64 `.xdata` unwind codes are stored in
  **reverse-prologue order**, and the superseded decoder chained them the other way. **The
  reusable method: do not reason about a bit-level spec from memory — decode real `.xdata`
  against a disassembled prologue.** Corollary worth internalising: **a fix's RATIONALE can be
  wrong even when the fix is right**, and the wrong rationale costs the next reader.
- **A return address ONE PAST the function end** `[§9.93]` — when a `bl` is the last instruction
  (callee is noreturn, so LLVM emits no trailing instruction), the return address lands outside
  the function and the lookup fails. **Fix (arch-standard): look up `retaddr - 1`** in the arm64
  `RtlDispatchException` and `RtlUnwindEx` frame walks.
- **A garbage frame size wedges the boot, and it is NOT a fault storm** `[§9.69]`. Enabling the
  fault-tolerant copy on arm64 hung with no bugcheck: `RtlVirtualUnwind` decoded a garbage frame
  size → garbage SP → the transfer-to-handler faulted on the bad SP → **infinite
  exception-vector re-entry.** Two hypotheses falsified first (a DUMMY_PSEH "silent-skip crutch",
  and a recursive fault storm overflowing the stack). A *software* raise passes — only a real
  hardware fault exercises the path, which is why the self-test mattered.
- **Cross-module table-SEH drops every `__except` reached through a callee whose call site sits
  at its epilog boundary** `[§9.48]` — one line in `unwind_decode.rs`. It hid because the
  existing PoC only unwound *ntdll* frames. The `__finally` half needs `EstablisherFrame == x29`.
- **The kernel-mode SEH *resume* path used `NtContinue`** `[§9.92]`, which clears the shallow
  raise tests. Remaining in that cluster: `KeMutex` + `SeInheritance` raise from **inside**
  `KeWaitForSingleObject`; `ExHardError` is a *distinct* pool illegal-instruction (OPEN); and
  `MmSection` is an in-kernel **wedge**, not a raise-escape (OPEN).
  **A "one root, N tests" cluster label is a HYPOTHESIS** — un-mask each test separately.
- **`RtlWalkFrameChain(NULL, …)` was a cross-arch NULL-store AV**; `RtlCaptureStackBackTrace
  (BackTrace=NULL)` BUGCHECKs 0x1E and **aborted the whole i386 kmtest sweep** (52 → 74 tests
  once guarded) `[§9.105a]`. The quarantine note's stated root cause was **wrong** and cost real
  time; the smoking gun was an **off-by-one in the trace, not an address**. The guard is
  deliberately **cfg-gated to i386 and self-retiring** — guarding all arches measurably costs.
- **arm64 `RtlWalkFrameChain` started its walk at `sp`, not `x29`.** The generic walk reads
  `[frame]` = caller's frame and `[frame + ptr]` = return address: the x86 EBP chain, and on
  AArch64 exactly the x29 frame record. Starting at `sp` read locals as frame records, so it
  returned 0 frames (RtlStackKM 13/27, user-mode RtlStack 16/24, in rtlk and ntdll alike). Two
  more x86-isms rode along: the return address was read as a 32-bit `ULONG`, and the kernel
  walk's "stop at user mode" test was `Eip & 0x80000000`; on 64-bit it is the top bit.
- **arm64 user-mode SEH never delivers first-chance** — `RtlRaiseException` is unimplemented for
  arm64 (OPEN; needs a `#[naked]` capture stub).

### arm64 raised every refused page fault as ACCESS_VIOLATION
**Symptom.** arm64 user-mode RtlException got `0xc0000005` where it expects
STATUS_STACK_OVERFLOW (`RtlException.c:171`), although MM had logged "Close to our death".

**Cause.** The data-abort handler in `ke/arm64/trap.rs` discarded MmAccessFault's status
and raised STATUS_ACCESS_VIOLATION whenever it was negative. Guard-page and stack-overflow
refusals return their own codes, and Windows raises them as those codes, as do our i386
(`traphdlr.rs`) and amd64 handlers.

**Fix.** Raise MmAccessFault's status when it is GUARD_PAGE_VIOLATION or STACK_OVERFLOW,
and AV otherwise.

### An uninitialised PFN `CacheAttribute` turns every `VirtualProtect`ed page into DEVICE memory
`MiInitializePfn` (and the `AndMakePteValid` / `ForOtherProcess` variants) never set
`u3.e1.CacheAttribute` — faithfully, because upstream ReactOS's C doesn't either. **`MiNonCached`
is 0**, so a page coming off the free list reads as *deliberately uncached* when nobody ever
decided anything. `MiFlushTbAndCapture` consults that field on **every protection change** and
force-ORs `MM_NOCACHE` onto the mask for a `MiNonCached` PFN, so a plain `VirtualProtect` on
private memory silently rewrites the page uncached.

On x86 that costs only performance, which is why it survived for years. On arm64 `MM_NOCACHE`
selects MAIR **AttrIndx 1 = Device-nGnRnE**, where *every unaligned access alignment-faults* —
and unaligned stores are completely ordinary in x86 code an emulator is translating. The fix is
to set `MiCached` in the three init paths, which is what Windows does; genuinely uncached pages
(MMIO) never come through them — `MmMapIoSpace` and the MDL paths set the attribute explicitly.

Two recognition rules fall out of it:

- **A zero-valued enum member is not a default, it is an assertion.** `MiNonCached == 0` means
  "uninitialised" and "the caller chose uncached" are the same bit pattern, so every consumer
  believes a decision that was never made. Suspect this whenever a field is only ever *read*.
- **Decode the PTE, don't trust the protection.** `[ALIGN] FAR=… PTE=… MAIR=…` gives you the
  answer directly: `AttrIndx = PTE[4:2]`, index it into `MAIR_EL1` (ours is `0x004400FF`:
  0=Normal-WB, 1=Device-nGnRnE, 2=Normal-NC). A page that is *architecturally* Normal but
  *mapped* Device faults on exactly the accesses Normal memory permits, so the symptom looks
  like a CPU bug rather than a mapping bug. The tell is a fault that **repeats at a pinned PC**:
  the handler un-protects, resumes, and the same unaligned store faults again forever.

**The opcode tells you which of the two you have, and this is the whole triage.** An unaligned
`ldar`/`stlr`/`ldxr` faults on *any* memory type — that is an ordinary unaligned ATOMIC (x86
permits them, AArch64 does not) and the emulator's own handler is supposed to absorb it. An
unaligned **plain** `ldr`/`str` faulting means the page is Device, full stop, because Normal
memory permits it. Measured across the arm64 WoW64 ladder: before the fix, 6–14 `[ALIGN]` per
boot, `PTE=…447` (AttrIndx 1) with `OPC=0xB83F6AB4` — a plain `str`; after, 0–1 per boot,
`PTE=…4C3` (AttrIndx 0) with `OPC=0x88DFFE85` — `ldar`, absorbed and the run passes. So the
whole class collapsed to the one case that is *supposed* to happen.

### Calibrating against interrupt ARRIVAL measures TCG latency, not the clock
Symptom: `QueryPerformanceCounter`/`clock()` drift against system time by a different amount
every boot (Wine ucrtbase misc.c:1355 had `clock()` 0.5-3 s short over a few seconds). Cause:
the APIC HAL's QPC is the raw TSC at a rate `HalpInitializeTsc` derived from four 1/1024 s RTC
interrupts. Under TCG an interrupt is delivered late whenever the host is busy, a late tick
inflates its sample by up to 1.5x, and a 3 ms window cannot average that out: one image
calibrated 4.23 to 7.95 GHz against a 4.20 GHz TSC. Fix: measure against something you READ,
not something that interrupts you. `tsc.rs` polls a PIT channel-2 one-shot for 50 ms (Linux's
`pit_calibrate_tsc`) and got 4.2023-4.2031 GHz on every boot of both x86 arches; the boot log
prints `[HAL] TSC ... kHz` with the RTC estimate beside it. Any other "count ticks between
interrupts" calibration in the tree has the same weakness under TCG.

### Real hardware: what QEMU's TCG does not model
Every one of these passed smoke ×N and failed on the first physical board (Raspberry Pi 4,
2026-09-25/26). On arm64, a green QEMU run is necessary and nowhere near sufficient.
- **Idle `WFE` with IRQs masked never wakes.** Symptom: desktop up, then ~70 s later the clock
  freezes, serial goes silent, no bugcheck; a raw-UART tick heartbeat stops too. Cause: the
  idle loop masked IRQs (`daifset #2`) and ran `wfe` when nothing was ready. A masked IRQ is
  not a WFE wake-up event (it is for WFI), and nothing issued `SEV` or enabled the timer event
  stream, so the core slept forever with the tick pending. TCG implements WFE as a yield. The
  ~70 s was the zero-page thread: it keeps the CPU busy until all free RAM is zeroed, and the
  first truly idle moment was fatal. Fix: `wfi`. What found it: sampling the tick's health from
  IRQ entry, user traps AND the idle loop, and all three staying silent — "the CPU is in
  none of those places" was the answer. Do not use WFE without an explicit `SEV` protocol.
- **Non-shareable PTEs: cross-core atomics silently lose updates.** Symptom: the MP kernel on
  4 cores hung in `KeIpiGenericCall` with `Count=2` though all three targets had executed their
  `fetch_sub` (another run: the call completed with the wrong result set). Cause: `ValidKernelPte`
  and `MmProtectToPteMask` left SH (bits [9:8]) at 0b00, so every page the memory manager mapped
  was Non-shareable; v8.0 LDXR/STXR from different cores on such memory need not be coherent.
  TCG makes every atomic atomic. Fix: SH = Inner Shareable on all Normal memory (stubs.rs mask,
  `arm/init.rs` templates, the hyperspace template). Mapping one PA with two shareabilities is
  itself a bug, so fix every template, not just the one that bit.
- **Secondary cores arrive at EL2, via SMC.** The PSCI conduit is the FADT's to state
  (`ARM_BOOT_ARCH`: QEMU says HVC, TF-A on a Pi says SMC; the wrong one jumps into dead vectors),
  and TF-A starts a `CPU_ON` core at NS-EL2 whenever EL2 exists. The AP trampoline
  (`hal-rust/src/arm64/mpboot.rs`) reads both from ACPI and drops to EL1 exactly as the loader
  does for the boot CPU.
- **PL011 FIFO overrun.** A bare store to the data register drops bytes once the 16–32 byte
  FIFO fills; TCG drains instantly. Serial "stopped" mid-line and was misread as the kernel
  stopping. Every debug byte goes through `Arm64UartPutChar` (TXFF-bounded); enforced by
  `scan_raw_uart_writes`.
- **A PTE attribute the MAIR doesn't mean.** `MI_PAGE_DISABLE_CACHE` set x86 PCD bits that
  selected MAIR slot 0 (Normal WB) on arm64, so the UART and GIC were cached. TCG ignores
  memory attributes. Fixed in `mm.rs` to AttrIndx 1 (Device) / 2 (Normal-NC).
  The flip side: a caller that disables caching on **RAM**, where x86 PCD only means
  "don't pollute the cache", now gets Device memory. `MiMapPagesInZeroSpace` did, and the
  first `dc zva` in `KeZeroPages` alignment-faulted in `MmZeroPageThread` on a Raspberry
  Pi 4 (BUGCHECK 0x1E, 0x80000002, ESR DFSC 0x21) while QEMU booted green. RAM stays
  Normal WB on arm64; Device-mapping it also aliases the page's WB mappings.
- **I/D cache incoherence.** Code paged in by `IoPageRead` (or relocated by the loader) sits in
  the D-cache; the I-side fetches stale RAM (zeros decode as `UDF`, ESR EC=0). Clean to PoU and
  invalidate the I-cache after writing code (`KeSweepICache`). TCG has no caches.
- **Every QEMU smoke boot has a NIC; the board may not.** QEMU attaches a default NIC when the
  command line names none, and no smoke config passes `-nic none`, so plain smoke has always
  had virtio-net (arm64) or e1000 (x86), whatever a docstring says. So a "no adapter" path never
  runs in QEMU. On the Pi 4 (GENET, which netstack does not drive) the engine worker exited
  while TDI kept pending IRPs into its dead inbox, and a loopback `sendto` hung forever.
  Reproduce NIC-less in QEMU with `VIBEOS_QEMU_EXTRA_ARGS="-nic user,model=rtl8139"` (a NIC
  nothing drives). Not `-nic none`: that renumbers PCI, the efivars boot entry then names the
  wrong device, and the firmware drops to the Shell.
- **Probing a fixed address for a device finds one on any board where memory answers.**
  Symptom: the Pi 5 installs ~100 PCI devices whose IDs are ASCII (`VEN_706F`,
  `SUBSYS_72656666`), floods serial with `rundll32` spawns, and loses 10-30% of pings. Cause:
  with no MCFG, the arm64 HAL read QEMU virt's fixed ECAM bases and accepted any vendor word
  other than 0xFFFF; on the Pi 5 both 0x3F00_0000 (RAM) and 0x40_1000_0000 answer, so pci.sys
  enumerated, and wrote config cycles into, whatever was there. Fix: take the base from the
  MCFG, and probe only on QEMU (XSDT OEM "BOCHS "). A "not all-ones" probe only proves
  absence on a bus that returns all-ones; never use one to prove presence at an address no
  table gave you. Related trap: **a table the loader saw can be gone by the time the kernel
  looks.** On the Pi 5 the MCFG's signature is zeroed after freeldr reads it (OEM, length and
  body intact; no code of ours writes it, so suspect the firmware at ExitBootServices), so
  freeldr logs `MCFG OEM "RPIFDN"` and the HAL finds no MCFG. Log signatures
  and OEM IDs from the kernel side before trusting the loader's view.
- **An SError reported at `_enable` happened somewhere else, maybe in the loader.**
  Symptom: BUGCHECK 0x80, ESR EC=0x2F (`0xBE000011`), the PC on `_enable+4` in
  `KiSystemStartupBootStack`, every boot of the Pi 5. Cause: `_enable` is `daifclr #0xF`,
  the first time anything unmasks SError, so an SError left pending at ANY earlier point,
  including firmware and the loader at EL2, is delivered there. Here it was the loader's
  PCI detection reading an MCFG "ECAM" that was really the Broadcom PCIe controller's
  registers (00:00.0 read 0xDEADDEAD). QEMU's ECAM never aborts, so smoke cannot see it.
  How to find the access: bracket it with `ISR_EL1` (bit 8 = SError pending), which reads
  the state without taking it, printed at checkpoints from `EfiEntry` to the kernel
  handoff, then halve the window that flips 0 to 0x100. Five boots found it. Do not trust
  firmware ECAM on boards that are not SBSA: the loader keeps an MCFG quirk list
  (`freeldr-rust/src/arm64_serial_acpi.rs`) the way Linux's `pci_mcfg.c` does.
- **A pin the firmware never configured has its pad's output disabled.** Symptom: the Pi 5's
  GEM came up, but no PHY answered on MDIO after the driver pulsed the PHY's reset line (RP1
  GPIO 32). The pulse never left the chip: RP1 pads come out of reset with output-disable set
  (bit 7, `0xd6`), and only Linux's pinctrl clears it (`0x56`), so a reset sequence copied from
  the device tree does nothing under UEFI. Fix: clear the pad's OD bit (and set IE) before
  driving the pin (`netstack-rust/src/gem.rs` `reset_phy`). Read the pad, the function select and
  the RIO bits on both sides before guessing.
- **A PHY that advertises EEE to a MAC driver that ignores LPI loses frames before the MAC.**
  Symptom: the Pi 5 drops ~8% of pings in a rhythm (one frame every 2.5 s, bursts every
  ~14 s); the sender's capture shows each lost request on the wire, the driver never sees it,
  and the MAC counts no FCS, buffer or overrun error. Cause: the BCM54213PE advertises Energy
  Efficient Ethernet out of reset (MMD 7.60 = 0x6), so the link enters low-power idle between
  frames. Fix: clear the advertisement before restarting auto-negotiation unless the driver
  implements LPI (Linux's phylib applies the same rule). How it was found: per-sequence
  counts at the driver plus a capture on a second LAN host split "never arrived" from
  "arrived, not answered" from "answered, lost"; only then was there one place to look.
- **A self-test with the emulator's addresses baked in breaks the real network it runs on.**
  netstack's self-tests targeted QEMU slirp's 10.0.2.2/.3/.100; on the Pi 5 one programmed a
  default route via 10.0.2.2, and the endless ARP for it starved smoltcp's interface-wide
  neighbor-discovery rate limit, dropping replies to real peers. Take targets from the
  lease; gate harness-only peers on actually being on slirp.
- **A Cadence GEM can go idle with a frame queued.** If the TX DMA reads the next descriptor
  while it is still CPU-owned, it stops, and a TSTART written as it finished the previous frame
  is ignored; the frame then waits for the next send. The log shows `TSR` 0x21 (used bit read,
  complete) with `TGO` clear and a CPU-released descriptor at the consumer index. Fix: from the
  poll path, re-issue TSTART whenever frames are outstanding and `TGO` is clear, as Linux's
  `macb_tx_restart` does.
- **A UART print inside a trap costs ~90 ms per KB at 115200 baud.** QEMU's UART is instant, so
  per-fault diagnostics are free there. FEX takes ~1,200 alignment faults per ladder boot by
  design (unaligned `STLR`/`LDAR` on an A72, which has no LSE2; QEMU raises them too), and the
  ~1 KB `[UEXC]`+`[ALIGN]` record per fault was minutes of serial time on the board. Those
  codes are now capped after 32 records (tripwire `UEXCVERBOSE` restores all). Before timing
  anything on hardware, count what the trap path prints.
  The same cost applies outside traps: the per-thread and per-process breadcrumbs (`[PS]`
  thread/process creation and exit, `[MM] InitProcAS`, `[IRQL-CHK]`, the `[APC]` frame dump)
  were ~20 lines per thread and, on the Pi 5, 70-80% of the serial output after the desktop
  appeared; gating them took first-minute ping loss from 12.5% to 3.3%. They now print only
  when the boot options carry `PROCTRACE` (`ps-rust/src/trace.rs`, flag `VibeProcTrace` in
  ntoskrnl-rust `shim_exports.rs`). Still printed without it: the first
  `PspUserThreadStartup: returning` (a smoke milestone) and the exit trace of a thread that
  exits non-zero (`tools/ucrt_tier2_sweep.py` reads it).

### arm64 bring-up bugs worth recognising again
- **`0xE3 RESOURCE_NOT_OWNED` (#43) was a fastfat shim testing the wrong WAIT bit.**
  Symptom: arm64 `0xE3 (Resource, Thread, 0, 3)`, a shared release of an ERESOURCE that is
  completely idle (no owner, `ActiveEntries 0`). Rare normally, 4 in 5 kmtest boots once
  delay-load moved DLL page-ins to arbitrary later points. Cause: `rust_cohab_stub.c`
  hard-coded `FAT_IRP_CTX_FLAG_WAIT` as `0x1`, which is `IRP_CONTEXT_FLAG_DISABLE_DIRTY`; the
  real WAIT bit is `0x2`. Every global/VCB/FCB acquire through that shim therefore ran
  non-blocking. `FatCommonCleanup` ignores the result of its FCB acquire, because in the C it
  always blocks. So while a page fault held the FCB exclusively (`MmNotPresentFaultSectionView`
  → `FsRtlAcquireFileExclusive`), cleanup on another thread "released" it, and the fault's own
  `FsRtlReleaseFile` then found it idle. Found by making the resource record its LAST releaser
  (caller PC and thread in `ERESOURCE.Reserved2`/`Address`, arm64 only, printed on the 0xE3
  and resolved with `KiPcToFileHeader`): four captures, all `prev.caller =
  fastfat.sys+0x4d068` = `FatCommonCleanup`'s `FatReleaseFcb`, on another thread. Fix: the
  shim takes the flag from `rust_cohab_fat.c`, which is built against the real `fatstruc.h`,
  exactly as it already did for the struct offsets. The lesson: a hand-written shim that
  hard-codes a header constant is the same hazard as one that hard-codes an offset.
  Nothing checks it, and when it is wrong the code usually still runs.
  The same shim's `FatAcquireExclusiveFcb` stood in for a function the translation had
  dropped, and dropped half of it again: no `OutstandingAsyncWrites` drain and no
  `FatVerifyOperationIsLegal`, so an exclusive acquirer (truncate, set-EOF, cleanup, flush)
  could run under a non-cached async write still landing. It is ported into `resrcsup.rs` next
  to its shared siblings, which always had the drain (2026-09-25). When a shim stands in for a
  dropped function, diff it against the C BODY, not just the signature.
- **Nothing saved FP/SIMD state across arm64 traps or context switches.** `kiinit.rs`
  enables FP on every CPU and the compiler vectorizes kernel code (memcpy, struct zeroing,
  frame copies), but the vectors saved only x0–x30, and `KiSwapContext`/`KiCallUserMode` only
  x19–x30. Fixed: `NEON_SAVE`/`NEON_RESTORE` of q0–q31 plus FPCR/FPSR on every returning
  vector entry (`trap.S`, placed below the frames so the trap frame's position is unchanged),
  and d8–d15 in the switch and callout frames. This was a real latent bug, but it was NOT the
  cause of #43: a 10-round soak with it in place still hit 0xE3 four times. Do not re-read
  the 3/3 clean run that preceded that soak as evidence.
  The same gap had a second exit, closed 2026-09-25. `NtContinue` and `NtRaiseException` leave
  through `KiExceptionExit`, which does `mov sp, TrapFrame; b KiTrapReturn` and so never reaches
  `NEON_RESTORE`: a thread resumed after an exception got whatever V registers the kernel last
  used, not its own. `KiDispatchException` and `KiInitializeUserApc` also asked for
  CONTROL|INTEGER only, where Windows asks for `CONTEXT_FULL`, so V never reached a handler
  either. Fix: `NEON_SAVE` records the area's distance below its trap frame in
  `KTRAP_FRAME.VfpState` (0 = no area, cleared again by `NEON_RESTORE`).
  `KeTrapFrameToContext`/`KeContextToTrapFrame` convert V0–V31/FPCR/FPSR through that area,
  and `KiExceptionExit` reloads from it. The user-callback frame is a byte COPY of the trap
  frame, so it copied the distance too, which is wrong measured from the copy; it clears it.
  The general rule: a frame field that locates something by OFFSET is wrong in every copy of
  that frame. Regression check: `tools/payloads/neonctx` (arm64), which faults with a pattern in
  v0–v31 and resumes from a vectored handler. It passes 20/20 with the fix; with the fix
  disabled it fails every round, showing exactly the handler's scribbled registers.
- **A dropped C `ASSERT` is a machine freeze on arm64, not a lost debug check.** Symptom: a
  boot wedges with a vCPU at EL1, PC parked, DAIF all masked, no bugcheck and no timer; the
  faulting VA is a user address, hardware reports a level-3 translation fault (EC 0x25,
  DFSC 0x07), and the PTE software reads for that same VA has `Valid = 1`. Cause:
  `MI_MAKE_HARDWARE_PTE_USER` was translated without the four ASSERTs the C original opens
  with -- the ones commented *"check that we are not setting valid a page that should not be"*
  (`ASSERT(ProtectionMask & MM_PROTECT_ACCESS)` and friends). `MM_PROTECT_ACCESS` is 7, so
  `mask & 7 == 0` selects exactly the four rows of `MmProtectToPteMask` that are zero
  (zero-access, no-access, guard, decommit). On x86 a zero row still leaves a translatable
  page -- the helper's own `Valid | User | PFN` is a complete present PTE -- so the bug degrades
  to a wrongly READABLE page and hides. On arm64 that table is the ONLY source of bit 1
  (`NotLargePage`) and bit 10 (AF), so the same mask yields `Valid = 1` with descriptor type
  `0b01`, which is RESERVED at level 3: the MMU refuses the translation, `MmAccessFault` reads
  `Valid = 1` and reports `STATUS_SUCCESS`, and the trap returns to the same instruction
  forever. Both are telling the truth about different fields of one word. Fix: restore the
  assert as a real runtime guard, centrally (`ntkrnl_sys::mm::mi_user_pte_may_be_valid`) -- a
  protection granting no access leaves the entry not-present, which is what the mask asked for,
  so the fault takes the invalid path and the thread gets a clean access violation instead of
  taking the box down. The reusable half: an `ASSERT` dropped in translation is not equivalent
  to a dropped debug print. It encodes a precondition another arch enforces in *hardware*, so
  the same wrong value that is survivable on x86 is unrecoverable on arm64. `scan_assert_to_ub`
  does not cover this -- it catches an assert lowered to `unreachable_unchecked()`, not one
  deleted outright, and its oracle (rustconv's trailing C comments) is absent from hand-written
  bridge modules like `ARM3/helpers.rs` anyway. `tools/scan_dropped_asserts.py` now gates this
  class -- it pairs the C `FORCEINLINE` against its same-named Rust twin cross-file and reports
  fewer asserts on the Rust side -- but it opened with 89 findings, so a helper you are about to
  trust may well be one of them. Grep the C for `ASSERT` before calling a translated MM/KE
  helper faithful.
  **Know which hang you are now in.** Restoring the guard did NOT make the boot pass — it
  converted an unobservable freeze (EL1, DAIF all masked, PC parked, no timer, no bugcheck,
  nothing downstream can see it) into a clean `BUGCHECK 0x1E` with a full stack. Neither boots,
  but they are very different debugging positions, and the second one is reachable by every
  instrument we own. Two traps in reading the second: the flight recorder's ~1.1M
  `ws-lock-excl`/`ws-unlock-excl` pairs are HISTORY from before the fault, not a live livelock
  (this entry said otherwise for a day), and the harness verdict `FROZEN — every vCPU PC is
  identical` is just the post-bugcheck halt. Symbolicate the parked PC before theorising about
  it: ours was `xHalHaltSystem+8`, the machine having stopped correctly. Worked example —
  `20260906-190514-conformance-arm64/summary.json` records bugcheck `0x1E` and its sampled PC
  `0xfffff80042205e7c` resolves into that halt path in the matching binary. A recorder's event
  count describes preceding activity, never what the stopped CPU is doing now; re-derive the
  live PC and its image relocation before naming a hang mechanism from one. Expect this shape
  whenever you refuse a bad value inside a helper whose caller has no error return: the caller
  cannot observe the refusal, so it retries. That is a step forward, not a fix, and the real repair belongs where
  the bad value is chosen.
- **"Software says valid, hardware says translation fault" has two causes on arm64, and they
  need opposite fixes.** Either the entry was never published to the page-table walker (a
  separate observer from this core's loads -- needs `dsb ishst`; see `MI_WRITE_VALID_PTE`), or
  the entry is published and *malformed*. Dump the PTE through the self-map before choosing: a
  well-formed user page reads `0x...443` (Valid, NotLargePage, Owner, AF), a malformed one
  `0x...041`. Guessing wrong costs a build-and-soak cycle per guess.
- **A page the working-set trimmer aged faults forever: arm64 has no hardware Access Flag.**
  Symptom: arm64 under memory pressure (about 25 x86-64 guests into an appstorm64 sweep) goes
  silent: the serial stops, the kernel census included, and apps launched just before it stop
  making windows. gdb on the stub shows one vCPU at EL0 with `ESR_EL1 = 0x8200000b`: an
  instruction abort, IFSC 0x0B, an **access-flag** fault at level 3, on a PC in ntdll, and
  `ELR == FAR` on every sample. Cause: `TrimWsList` (wslist.rs) ages a page by clearing
  `PTE_ACCESSED`. On x86 the CPU sets the bit again. arm64 runs without hardware AF
  management, so the next touch faults on a still-VALID PTE. Every Mm path that sees a valid
  PTE (`MmArmAccessFault`, RosMm's `MmNotPresentFaultSectionView`) returns "spurious, retry"
  without setting AF, and the retry faults again. Fix: `ki_set_access_flag` in
  `KiSynchronousExceptionHandler` (trap.rs). It is the one place that knows the fault is an AF
  fault (FSC 0x08-0x0B), so it sets AF on the faulting level's descriptor by compare-exchange,
  which covers every Mm path. **A bit that hardware maintains on x86 and software maintains on
  arm64 needs a software path to set it, not just one to clear it.**
- **A written page made read-only pages out as CLEAN on arm64, and comes back from the file.**
  Symptom: after the AF fix above let a long appstorm64 sweep keep running, native processes
  (a dhcpcsvc thread, then csrss, so bugcheck 0xF4) took PC-alignment faults (`ESR
  0x8A000000`, EC 0x22) at small odd addresses such as `0xAA462`. Those are IMAGE_IMPORT_BY_NAME
  RVAs: the call went through an UNBOUND import slot. Cause: arm64 has no hardware dirty bit.
  "Dirty" is NotDirty (AP[2]) clear, i.e. hardware-writable. RosMm's arm64 `MmSetPageProtect`
  built the new PTE from scratch, so the loader's bound IAT (written, then made read-only) read
  clean. i386 copies its Dirty bit across a protection change. Under memory pressure
  `MmPageOutPhysicalAddress` saw a private copy-on-write page that was "clean" with no swap
  entry, freed it, and the next fault re-read the original from the image. Fix: a sticky software
  dirty bit (`PTE_SOFTWARE_DIRTY`, the MMU-ignored OsAvailable bit 57) that `MmSetPageProtect`
  sets when it reprotects a dirty page. `MI_PTE_IS_DIRTY` (ARM3/helpers.rs) is the one dirty
  test, used by `TrimWsList`, ARM3's `MI_IS_PAGE_DIRTY` and RosMm's `WasDirty`. **Same lesson as
  the AF entry: list every bit x86 hardware keeps up to date, and give each one a software path
  on arm64.**
- **A touched page made PAGE_NOACCESS reads back as a PROTOTYPE PTE on arm64; the machine wedges
  spinning on `MmPfnLock`.** Symptom: one process doing `VirtualProtect(PAGE_NOACCESS)` on pages it
  has used (page heap's guard pages did it at once) and the whole arm64 VM goes silent. gdb: the
  vCPU spins in `KeAcquireSpinLockRaiseToDpc` on `MmPfnLock`, whose owner word names a DIFFERENT
  thread, so on one CPU nothing can release it. That thread's saved stack: `NtProtectVirtualMemory`
  → `MiGetPageProtection` (PFN lock held) → kernel data abort → `MmAccessFault` blocked on the
  address-space push lock: a context switch with a spinlock held. Cause: `MiProtectVirtualMemory`'s
  NOACCESS branch makes the transition PTE IN PLACE, as the C does: clear Valid, set Transition and
  Protection, keep every other bit. On x86 no hardware bit lands on a software field that matters.
  On arm64 hardware bit 10 is the Access Flag and software bit 10 is Prototype, so the next
  `MiGetPageProtection` took the prototype path and read through a garbage pointer with the PFN
  lock held. The same lines also dropped the dirty bit, sending a written page to the standby
  list as clean. Fix (virtual.rs): mark the PFN modified if `MI_PTE_IS_DIRTY`, then build the
  transition PTE from scratch with `MI_MAKE_TRANSITION_PTE`. **Converting a hardware PTE to a
  software one in place inherits every hardware bit into a software field; on arm64 build the
  software PTE from zero.**
- **An EL1 instruction fetch on a user page loops silently forever — the fault handler called it
  spurious.** Symptom: a ~2% arm64 boot wedge with no bugcheck, no serial, every timed wait
  dead, every vCPU sample at the same user-range PC (`0x10000`) at EL1h; the whole box reads
  FROZEN. Cause: `KiSynchronousExceptionHandler` (trap.rs) sent every same-EL instruction abort
  to `MmAccessFault`, and `MmArmAccessFault`'s valid-PTE path bugchecks an instruction fetch only
  when the PTE says NOT executable (UXN, bit 54); a page that is *user*-executable passes and it
  returns `STATUS_SUCCESS` — "spurious, retry". AArch64 makes every EL0-writable page implicitly
  PXN, so EL1 can never execute it, and the retry faults at the same PC without end. Fix: a
  same-EL instruction abort (EC 0x21) on a VA below `MmUserProbeAddress`, or with a permission
  IFSC, never goes to paging — it is dispatched as a kernel access violation and bugchecks with
  the frame plus `[KSTKW]`, the kernel-range words on the faulting stack (a wild `br` leaves LR
  useless; the callers' return addresses above SP are the only route back to the jumper).
  **A second swallowing path, same function (task #39).** Dispatching the fetch AV was not
  enough. `KiDispatchException`'s user-address data-probe fixup accepted *every* access
  violation, execute faults included (`ExceptionInformation[0] == 8`). It read the
  inaccessible instruction as data, sometimes zeroed registers from its bits, advanced PC by
  four and returned — so the recorded PC is wherever that walk ended, not the original bad
  branch target. Five saved captures all end at `0x250000` for this reason. It is in the
  failing binary as well: PE VA `0x414494` tests the fault address without reading the access
  type at exception-record offset `0x20`, `0x4144f4` adds four to PC, `0x414574` can zero LR.
  Fix: exclude execute faults from the fixup, and dump the trap's LR and integer registers at
  the first unhandled fault. Excluding them exposes an EARLIER fault — patched runs stop at an
  EL1 instruction abort with PC, LR and FP all zero (`ESR=0x86000007`) in `lsass.exe`, with the
  semaphore-release frame still on the stack, while the same-commit control keeps the old
  `0x250000` undefined-instruction signature. The guard exposes the earlier fault; it does not
  repair the zero return. Binaries, indexes and logs for both sets are preserved under
  `~/vibeos-flake-farm/fails/smp39-20260906-{original,first-fault,control}/` — and preserving
  them is the point, because a capture left in `/tmp/vibeos-cli` is gone within days.
  The probe written to catch this exact frame — `KiTrapReturnProbe`, inspecting the EL0-return
  state at the `eret` — missed for three independent reasons: its call site is `#ifdef
  ARM64_TRAP_DEBUG` and that macro is **defined nowhere in the repo**, so it is dead source that
  reads like an armed instrument; it returns early unless the frame says EL0t, and this one says
  EL1h; and its bound is `pc < 0x10000`, a strict less-than at exactly the observed PC. **Before
  trusting an in-tree probe's silence, grep for its GUARD, not its code** — `#ifdef`, `cfg`,
  feature, and early-return each turn a probe into decoration, and all three did here.
  **Recognition rule: a "spurious fault, retry" return is only safe when the retry can succeed.
  An instruction-fetch permission fault has no paging remedy at any address — PXN/UXN is not a
  paged-out page — and a retry that cannot succeed is a hang with the handler's name on it.**
- **Every arm64 syscall ran with interrupts MASKED, end to end.** Taking any exception sets
  PSTATE.DAIF to all-masked in hardware; nothing in `KiEL0SynchronousEntry` (trap.S) undid it,
  so kernel-mode interrupt latency was bounded by the longest system call and every blocking
  syscall parked a DAIF-masked context on the swap chain. This was landmine #2 of the
  (archived) arm64-interrupts quest and had been known-and-deferred since 2026-07-05. Fix:
  `UNMASK_IRQ_FROM_SPSR` — re-enable **iff the interrupted context had them enabled**, reading
  the saved SPSR bit 7, which is exactly the rule x86 uses; a fault taken inside an IRQ handler
  or inside `KiTrapReturn`'s masked ELR/SPSR banking window therefore stays masked. It does not
  weaken IRQL: on this port IRQL is GIC-priority-backed (`GICC_PMR`) and no GIC line lives in
  the PASSIVE..DISPATCH band, so unmasking can only admit lines whose DIRQL genuinely exceeds
  the current IRQL. EL1 synchronous entry is still masked — a separate change.
  **Recognition rule: on a port where IRQL is priority-masked rather than DAIF-masked, DAIF
  belongs to exception entry/exit windows and nothing else. If a trap handler never touches it,
  it is running masked.**
- **A user-mode spinner was never preempted on arm64.** The only preemption point was
  `KfLowerIrql` crossing below DISPATCH in thread context, and a thread spinning at EL0
  never reaches it. The clock IRQ's own lowering runs at interrupt depth > 0 and is
  declined, so `QuantumEnd` and `NextThread` sat unread. On one CPU, any user spin-wait for
  a lock held by a preempted thread is a whole-guest livelock: ntdll_vista's threadpool
  worker spun in condvar `InternalLockCondVar`, and even the probe's own watchdog thread
  never ran. Fix: `KiEL0IrqPreempt`, called from `KiEL0IrqEntry` while the user's NEON
  state is still on the stack. It unmasks, raises to DISPATCH and lowers back, so the
  existing thread-context path does the switch. EL0 is the safe IRQ exit: PASSIVE, no
  kernel locks, and ELR/SPSR already in the frame.
- **PSTATE.DAIF is NOT per-thread state** `[§9.19]` — `KiSwapContext` doesn't save/restore it, so
  a context switch **leaked exception-entry DAIF into a new thread** → boot wedges with the
  serial completely silent. A masked-swap tripwire in `KiSwapContextResume` remains in tree.
  **The mirror bug is a dropped `cli`** in a C→Rust translation causing a callback-ERET
  IRQ-clobber race `[§9.54]`.
- **Every arm64 BUGCHECK wore a mask: the crash reporter crashed** `[§9.54]`
  (`KeGetBugMessageText` validation). **Triage rule: in any arm64 crash log, count the
  bugchecks — a second one is usually the reporter, and the first is the real one.**
- **ISR-queued DPCs never ran at desktop** `[§9.20]` — device-DPC delivery was gated on a starved
  `TimerRequest` flag; `KeInsertQueueDpc` returned 1 and nothing drained. Fix:
  `KiRetireDeviceDpcs` drains `DpcData[DPC_NORMAL]` unconditionally.
- **Desktop timer freeze = three stacked bugs** `[§9.21]`: `KeDelayExecutionThread` was still a
  busy-yield bring-up stub, explorer's main thread spun on a stuck `QS_PAINT` wake bit, and
  DISPATCH software-interrupt delivery was unimplemented.
- **Serial silent for ~95 s with the guest clock still ticking, then everything due fires at
  once** (a 10 s census missing nine scans, 30 s waits timing out together) — **arm64 had no
  preemption.** The DISPATCH softint expired timers but parked the woken thread in
  `Prcb->NextThread`, and only the idle loop or a voluntary wait ever switched to it;
  `QuantumEnd` was never read. So a thread that never blocks kept the CPU — here the
  **priority-0 zero-page thread**, clearing the free list after kmtest MmSection, once per
  arm64 conformance round. Fix: `KfLowerIrql` calls `KiDispatchPreemptArm64` on the crossing
  under DISPATCH (x86's DPC-interrupt tail). Three traps on the way:
  - It must decline when IRQs are masked.
  - The preempted thread must restore its own DAIF on resume. The first cut let the zero
    thread come back masked from an SVC-wait swap, and it froze the box: 63 s of host time,
    0.4 s of guest time.
  - `KeZeroPages` went through the CRT's byte-at-a-time memset, ~12 ms per 32-page batch under
    TCG, and every timer waited that long for the next crossing. It is `dc zva` now.

  **Tell it from a dead clock** by stamping serial with host time (conformance does this
  always) and reading `silence-samples.txt`, which the payload drain writes during any 20 s
  quiet that later recovers.
- **Desktop never repaints** `[§9.23]`: `gpdeskInputDesktop` stranded on the *Winlogon* desktop,
  and `SystemTime` was never seeded from the RTC (the "query the clock" block was dropped —
  arm64 needs the PL031 at `0x0901_0000`).
